outputs.L3:
The tracks vibrate and hum long before the train itself comes into view, a low tremor rising through the metal that serves as nature's own early warning system. Those who live and work near the rail line have learned to read these signs instinctively, feeling the approach of the great machine through the ground itself before any whistle sounds or plume of smoke appears on the horizon.

When this vibration is sensed, the response is immediate and practiced: people drop to all fours, lowering themselves to better navigate the uneven terrain surrounding the tracks. They make their way along the rails with careful steps or hop nimbly from sleeper to sleeper, their bodies attuned to a rhythm born of necessity and repetition. This is not mere caution but survival instinct, refined by generations of proximity to the iron beast that cuts through their land.

The train itself makes a singular journey, traveling from the deep interior toward the capital, its cars burdened with the spoils of the land—massive felled tree trunks stripped from the forest and raw bauxite ore torn from the earth. This is the train's purpose and its endpoint: to carry away what the interior yields and deliver it to the seat of power and commerce, where the true worth of these resources will be reckoned far from where they were extracted.

Throughout this journey, people keep their distance, wary and uncertain of the train's raw power. They understand, perhaps through hard experience or inherited warning, that this machine can flatten whatever lies in its path, destroying with an indifferent force anything unfortunate enough to be caught beneath its wheels. Its approach is heralded by a fierce, piercing whistle and clouds of ominous steam that seem to announce not just its presence but its dominance—a mechanical warning that demands respect and retreat.

The poem draws to its close by invoking the very trees whose trunks fill the train's cars: greenheart, mora, baromalli, purple heart, crabwood, kabakalli, and womara. In naming these native species, the verse forges a direct and poignant connection between the train's cargo and the land's natural bounty, reminding the reader that what rumbles along these tracks is not merely timber and ore, but the very substance of a landscape being steadily diminished, carried away piece by piece toward destinations that will never know the forests from which they came.
outputs.L4:
# Iron Road

In the timber-and-bauxite country
where the earth is opened like a wound
and the trees fall in the distance
like thunder without lightning,
the children know the train before they see it.

They feel it first—
a trembling in the rails,
a shiver that runs up through packed dirt
and into bare feet,
a language older than words.

They drop to all fours in the red dust,
press their ears to the iron,
listen to the metal sing
its low approaching hum,
a sound like the earth itself breathing hard.

Then they rise, arms out like wings,
and walk the rails in wobbling lines,
one foot then another,
balancing on the thin silver edge
between the ordinary world and speed,

imagining where it goes—
to the capital, they say,
where the tracks disappear into buildings
taller than any tree left standing,
where the ore becomes something else entirely,
something with a different name.

But underneath the wonder
is the fear they carry like a stone
in the pocket of their chests:
the train that flattens
whatever dares to wait too long—
a dropped coin, a stray dog,
the slow certainty of an ox cart
caught between one crossing and the next.

They have seen what is left after:
the metal folded like paper,
the terrible silence that follows
the terrible sound,
a roar like something ancient
uncaged and screaming down the line,
a battle cry with no enemy
but everything in its path.

And so they chant the names—
the trees that stood before the coming
of the rails, before the trucks,
before the deep red gashes
in the hillside where the bauxite gleams
like something torn from the body of the world:

*mahogany, greenheart, wallaba,
purpleheart, silverballi, crabwood—*

names that taste like home in the mouth,
names that root them to the ground
even as the ground gives way
beneath the weight of what is coming,
even as the whistle blows
and the children scatter
like birds before a storm,
carrying the names like seeds
back into the diminishing trees.
outputs.L5:
# The Long Train

The train stretched impossibly long across the horizon, its cars disappearing into the distance like a metal serpent winding through the countryside. Passengers boarding at the front had no way of knowing what awaited those seated dozens of cars back—different landscapes passing by their windows, different weather even, as the train moved through microclimates that shifted from sunny skies to gentle rain over its considerable length.

Conductors walked for what felt like hours to move from one end to the other, radioing ahead to colleagues they might not see in person for the entire journey. Some joked that the dining car staff had never met the crew who worked the observation deck, despite technically being coworkers on the same voyage.

The long train had become something of a local legend in the towns it passed through. Children would run alongside the tracks, waving at car after car after car, losing count somewhere around the fortieth or fiftieth carriage. Parents would tell stories of how the train seemed to take forever to pass completely—long enough to finish an entire meal, long enough for the sun to shift noticeably in the sky, long enough that some swore they'd aged slightly by the time the caboose finally rolled by.

There was something almost meditative about waiting for the long train to pass at a crossing. The rhythmic clacking of wheels on rails created a hypnotic pattern, a reminder that some journeys simply take time, that not everything can be rushed, and that the anticipation of an ending—watching for that final car, that last light—was its own peculiar pleasure, teaching patience to those willing to stand and wait.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about children in a timber and bauxite region who put their ears to train tracks to sense an approaching train, ending with a list of native hardwood tree names like greenheart and purple heart.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ears to the Rail**

Before the whistle, before the smoke
climbs over the bauxite hills like a slow orange animal,
the children already know.

They lie belly-down in the red dust,
cheek pressed to iron gone warm with morning,
and wait for the track to speak—

a hum first, faint as a held breath,
then a shiver that runs up through the jaw,
into the teeth, the small bones of the skull,
until the whole body becomes an ear.

This is how they read the world here,
in a country stitched together by rail lines
hauling ore from the earth's opened chest,
timber stacked like felled giants along the siding,
sap still weeping from the cut ends.

Their fathers work the pits where the ground is the color of rust and old blood.
Their mothers boil water the color of tea
because the river remembers the mines too.

But the children, ears to the rail,
are listening for something else—
not the train exactly, but the moment before it,
that pocket of knowing
that lives in the space between silence and arrival,
between the forest's breath and the machine's.

They have names for that silence.
They have names for everything that grows
taller than the trains, older than the mines,
roots reaching down further than any shaft:

greenheart, purpleheart, wallaba,
mora, kabukalli, letterwood,
bulletwood, silverballi, crabwood—

names heavy as the wood itself,
names that hold the shape of the hand
that first spoke them into the humid air,
long before iron ever touched this ground,
long before anyone thought to press an ear to anything
just to hear the future coming.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem evoking childhood memories of living near a railway line in Guyana, including sensory details of the trembling tracks, the danger of the train, and the surrounding rainforest trees.
counterfactuals.output:
# Where the Rails Ran Through

The tracks hummed before we saw it coming,
a low thrum rising through bare feet
pressed against warm steel—
we'd press our palms down too,
feeling the metal shiver like something alive,
a pulse beneath the rust and heat.

Auntie's voice would cut through the yard:
*Get back from the line, na!*
and we'd scatter to the grass edge,
hearts drumming faster than the rails,
watching the bend where green swallowed everything—
greenheart and purpleheart standing sentry,
their canopies stitched so tight
the sky came through in coins of light.

Then the train would break from that wall of leaves,
iron and smoke and thunder,
horn splitting the thick afternoon air,
scattering egrets from the swamp grass,
rattling mango trees until fruit
dropped like small bombs in the dirt.

We counted train cars like beads on a string,
dared each other closer to the edge,
felt the wind-slap of its passing
lift the hair from our necks,
the smell of hot metal and diesel
mixing with wet earth and crushed leaves,
with the sweetness of ripe guava
rotting somewhere in the bush.

After—always after—
the silence rushed back in
thicker than before,
cicadas reclaiming their static hum,
the tracks still ticking as they cooled,
and we'd lay coins we'd stolen from somewhere
flat against the rail,
waiting for tomorrow's train
to press them into something new,
something flattened and shining,
proof that we'd stood
right at the edge of danger
and the forest had watched us,
green and ancient and unbothered,
already forgetting
that we were ever there at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a piece of free verse that personifies a train as a powerful, almost mythic force—comparing it to oxen, a stampede, and a battle cry—while grounding it in a specific tropical landscape with bauxite cars and named local woods?
counterfactuals.output:
**Iron Beast of the Cutlass Hills**

It comes the way old bulls come—
low-shouldered, breath like furnace-smoke,
hooves that were never hooves
striking a rhythm older than the rails
laid down through cane and courida.

Ten thousand oxen could not match it,
yoked together, straining—
still they would fall behind
this thing of steel and stolen thunder
hauling its red cargo of bauxite,
mountains gutted and boxed,
rust-orange dust
settling like a plague over the tibisiri palms.

Listen: it comes like stampede,
like the memory of stampede,
when the savanna cattle broke loose
in the time before the fences,
before the mining trucks,
before this snake of cars
learned to run without legs, without lungs,
without anything but appetite—

and still it screams.

Not a whistle—a battle cry,
flung out over the greenheart and the wallaba,
over the silk cotton trees that flinch
in their old-god stillness,
over villages that feel it in their floorboards
before they hear it in their ears.

The bauxite cars rattle their bones,
red ore packed tight as sin,
and the whole assembly—
engine, cars, the ghost of every ox
that ever pulled a burden through this heat—
takes the curve past the tannia fields
like a war party riding for the coast,

leaving only sound behind it,
leaving only the shudder in the wood,
leaving the parrots screaming counter-cries
from the crowns of trees
that have stood since before iron
learned to move,
since before men decided
the earth's red marrow
was worth this kind of violence,
this kind of glory,
this kind of endless, ordinary thunder
rolling on through the Demerara dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about the anticipation and fear children feel before a train arrives, using imagery of balancing on rails, hiding from danger, and ending with a litany of exotic tree species names.
counterfactuals.output:
**Before the 4:15**

We walk the rail like tightrope saints,
arms out, sneakers kissing steel,
counting ties beneath our feet—
*one, two, don't fall, don't fall—*
the metal already humming
a song we feel in our teeth
before we hear it.

Somewhere past the bend
the world begins to shake its head.
A bird lifts off too early.
The gravel starts to whisper.
We know before we know,
the way deer know,
the way skin knows lightning
is close by the smell of it.

Off the rail. Into the ditch,
into the weeds gone gold and sharp,
crouched low where the cattails
hide our breathing,
where our hearts
go faster than the thing we're hiding from.

The whistle comes first, thin as a wire,
then the ground itself gives up its stillness,
then the great iron animal
tears past
so close we feel its wind
part our hair like a hand,
so loud the fear turns
inside out, becomes a kind of joy,
a scream we didn't know we'd saved for this.

And when it's gone—
when the tracks go quiet again,
when the ties stop singing
and the ditch lets us climb back out
with our knees full of green stain
and our hands still shaking—

we run for the shade,
we run for names that sound
like they were never afraid of anything:

baobab, jacaranda, kapok, banyan,
flame tree, dragon's blood, monkey puzzle,
ceiba, tamarind, sandalwood, ginkgo,
ombu, rosewood, silk floss, ironwood—

we say them like a chant,
like something that could carry us,
roots deep enough
to never have to move
when the next train comes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical, rhythmic poem in free verse form that explores a childhood ritual of listening for trains along undefined tracks, weaving in references to a capital city, felled trees, and industrial cargo like bauxite.
counterfactuals.output:
# Night Freight

We used to lie on the cooling porch boards
and listen for them—
the trains that ran on tracks
nobody could point to on a map,
tracks that existed only in the listening,
in the way sound travels through ground
before it travels through air.

My grandmother said the rails
ran clear to the capital,
that if you pressed your ear
hard enough to the earth
you could hear the whole city humming—
its glass and its arguments,
its lit windows arguing with the dark.

We never saw the trains.
Only heard them,
a low chord rising through the floorboards,
through the soles of our feet,
carrying what the land gave up:
felled trees stacked like sentences
nobody finished reading,
bauxite red as a wound
dug out of hills that used to hold birds,
now hollowed, now humming
with the weight of other people's want.

The cars would click by in the dark—
one two, one two, one two—
a rosary of iron,
each bead a ton of something
leaving before we understood
what leaving meant.

We counted them like sheep,
like the years we didn't have yet,
and somewhere past thirty
we always slept,
dreaming the ore, the timber,
the capital's far windows,
all of it moving through us
on rails we never found,
toward a place we never learned
except by listening,
except by lying still enough
to let the going-away
become a kind of lullaby.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
